newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian minister to face peers on sex allegations.
newsitem.headline: Belgian minister to face peers on sex allegations.

text.p: Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, centre of a public storm over allegations he had sex with under-age boys, will be offered a chance to defend himself before a commission of fellow parliamentarians.

The Belgian parliament decided on Tuesday to set up an all-party commission -- a first step in a formal procedure which could result in the lifting of the minister's constitutional immunity from prosecution and in his indictment.
Di Rupo will be allowed to testify before the 11-member panel and rebutt the paedophilia allegations, possibly with his lawyer at his side.
Di Rupo, a francophone Socialist, supports the procedure, saying it will give him access to investigators' files and allow him to find out who is accusing him.
So far the allegations, vehemently denied by Di Rupo, have only appeared in the Belgian press. The minister has not denied he is homosexual.
In Belgium homosexuality is allowed by law, but sex with children younger than 16 is outlawed.

The commission will respond to a request from the Brussels public prosecutor that the dossier on Di Rupo be examined by his peers to judge whether information gathered by investigators is enough to send the minister to Belgium's highest court, the Cour de Cassation.
Only the Cour de Cassation can try ministers and ex-ministers.
The public prosecutor may appear before the commission, which can also hear additional witnesses. All sessions will be behind closed doors.
Parliament chairman Raymond Langendries said it was essential that contents of the dossier be kept secret and that the principle of presumption of innocence be respected.
The commission is to advise parliament formally on whether to approve the public prosecutor's request.
Under Belgian law a minister can be questioned, confronted by witnesses or prosecuted, and his property searched, only once a full session of the lower house has voted to lift his immunity.
A date for a parliamentary vote has not yet been set. A simple majority of the 150-seat house is needed to implement the commission's advice.
Parliament has three options when it comes to a vote:
-- It can adopt the prosecutor's request and bring Di Rupo before the Cour de Cassation. This would almost instantly end his career.
-- It can vote for a continuation of the investigation. This could be seen as a stay of execution but would remove none of the pressure on Di Rupo to consider his position in the cabinet.
-- It can reject the request, risking almost certain public charges of a cover-up.
Even before the commission examines the dossier, several party leaders have already said Di Rupo might be forced to resign as he could not function in the current climate.
But it will take the votes of the largest coalition party, Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's CVP Flemish Christian Democrats, to send Di Rupo before the court.
If the CVP does not support Di Rupo it could drive a wedge between them and their Socialist coalition partners and ultimately spell the end of the centre-left coalition.
